body_markdown:
Storage can create room when an adult child moves home to support an older family member who needs 24/7 in-home care. Put away furniture, boxes, seasonal items, and household overflow so bedrooms and shared living areas stay clear and create more accessible pathways for those dealing with mobility issues.


Storage can also help when an older parent moves in with family, a guest room becomes a caregiver room, or two households combine temporarily. A storage unit is a good place to hold overflow, but keep medication, medical information, personal records, financial documents, and daily essentials at home.


Here are some more tips for using storage to ease your transition into caring for an elderly loved one.


## **Elder Care Storage Essentials:**


- Use storage to put away extra furniture, household bins, seasonal décor, and lower-use belongings.


- Create room when an adult child moves home to provide overnight support, help with meals, or coordinate appointments.


- Clear a guest room when it needs to become a bedroom for an older parent or a live-in caregiver.


- Keep daily-use furniture, open pathways, and commonly used household items accessible at home.


- Sort household items into use now, pack away, donate, recycle, and revisit-later categories.


- Label every storage box with its room, contents, and access priority.


- Keep frequently retrieved boxes near the entrance of the storage unit.


- Leave a clear aisle through the unit for access.


- Keep medication, personal records, medical information, and daily essentials at home.

## **How Can Storage Help When You Move Home to Care for an Older Family Member?**


Storage helps when you move home by creating room for your belongings and the household’s changing needs. Put away furniture, boxes, seasonal items, and household overflow while keeping daily-use rooms easier to organize.


For example, a family may store a guest-room desk, bookcase, and extra boxes so an adult child has a bedroom while helping with meals, errands, appointments, and overnight support. Another family may put away a dining set or living-room furniture so an older parent can use a first-floor room.


Start with a shared plan for bedrooms, living areas, bathrooms, and entryways. Decide which items need to stay accessible, which items can move to storage, and which items no longer fit the household routine moving forward.


## **What Should You Put in Storage During an Elder Care Transition?**


Put away household items that are not needed every day. This can include extra furniture, seasonal décor, guest-room items, hobby supplies, duplicate kitchen items, and labeled moving boxes.


Removing lower-use items can make it easier to update a bedroom, keep common areas open, and create a more functional space for family members and caregivers.


**Items to pack away may include:**


- Guest-room beds, desks, dressers, and shelving


- Extra chairs, side tables, and décor


- Seasonal décor and clothing


- Books and wall décor


- Hobby supplies


- Duplicate kitchen items after households combine


- Labeled household bins


- Furniture that does not fit the updated room layout


- Boxes from an adult child moving back home


- Items from a spare room becoming a caregiver room or bedroom


Keep daily-use furniture, medication, personal records, and household essentials at home.


## **How Do You Create Room for 24/7 In-Home Care?**


Create room for 24/7 in-home care by clearing a bedroom or shared living area of lower-use furniture and household overflow. Keep the home organized around the rooms and items family members and caregivers use regularly.


Start with the bedroom, bathroom, kitchen, entryway, and main living area. For example, move extra furniture from a downstairs room so it can serve as a bedroom, or clear a guest room so a family member can stay overnight and help with daily routines.


A storage unit can hold furniture, boxes, shelving, and other household items while you adjust the home layout. If you need to retrieve boxes around changing schedules,


[24/7](https://www.publicstorage.com/self-storage/24-hour-storage) access is available at select Public Storage locations.


## **How Should You Organize a Home During an Elder Care Transition?**


Organize the home by focusing on one room at a time and keeping high-use areas clear. Start with the bedroom, bathroom, kitchen, and main living area before sorting lower-priority spaces.


**Use these organization steps:**


1. List the rooms and household items that need attention.


2. Identify which room will serve as the primary bedroom, caregiver room, or shared living space.


3. Sort each item into use now, pack away, donate, recycle, or revisit later.


4. Keep daily-use belongings within easy reach.


5. Remove furniture and boxes that crowd common areas.


6. Create a shared household calendar, whiteboard, or notebook for appointments, errands, meal plans, and family tasks.


7. Label boxes before moving them into storage.


8. Reassess the layout after the household adjusts to the new routine.


## **What Storage Unit Size Helps During an Elder Care Transition?**


The right storage unit size depends on the number of boxes, furniture pieces, and household items you plan to put away. Measure large furniture before reserving and leave room for an aisle if you expect to retrieve items regularly.

## **How Can Drive-Up Storage Help During a Family Move?**


[Drive-up storage](https://www.publicstorage.com/self-storage/drive-up-storage) provides vehicle access near a ground-level unit door. It can help family members load and unload furniture, boxes, shelving, and bulky household items without carrying them through hallways or across the property.


Drive-up storage can be useful when moving a guest-room bed, dresser, desk, dining table, or extra living-room furniture while the household adjusts to an in-home care routine. More than 45% of Public Storage properties offer drive-up access units, totaling more than 2,200 locations.


## **Is Climate-Controlled Storage Useful for Household Items?**


[Climate-controlled storage](https://www.publicstorage.com/climate-controlled-storage) provides a more consistent indoor environment for furniture, clothing, books, photographs, electronics, and décor. It can help when you need to put away household items during a move, home update, or changing family routine.


More than 90% of Public Storage properties offer climate-controlled units, totaling more than 4,300 locations. Use labeled boxes or bins to keep the storage setup organized.


## **How Do You Keep a Storage Unit Organized for Family Access?**


Organize a storage unit by placing large furniture and long-term boxes along the back and side walls. Keep items you expect to retrieve sooner near the entrance, then maintain a clear aisle through the center.


**Use this layout:**


- Back wall: Large furniture and long-term household boxes


- Side walls: Labeled bins grouped by room or category


- Front area: Items to retrieve soon, such as seasonal bins, guest-room furniture, or extra household supplies


- Center aisle: Clear path from the entrance to the back wall


Create a simple inventory list with box numbers, contents, and locations. Take photos of the completed layout so different family members can easily find items without opening every box.


## **Create Room for Your Family’s Current Needs.**


Storage can help you put away furniture, household boxes, seasonal items, and lower-use belongings while you adjust a home for an older family member, a returning adult child, or an in-home care routine. Compare available unit sizes,


[drive-up storage](https://www.publicstorage.com/self-storage/drive-up-storage) , and


[climate-controlled storage](https://www.publicstorage.com/climate-controlled-storage) before reserving.


Room to adjust. Space to care.


## **Elder Care Storage FAQs**


**Can Self Storage Help When I Move Home to Care for an Older Family Member?**
Yes. Storage can create room for furniture, boxes, and household items while you organize bedrooms, shared living areas, and other spaces around your family’s current needs.


**What Should I Put in Storage During an Elder Care Transition?**
Put away items that are not needed every day, such as guest-room furniture, extra chairs, seasonal décor, hobby supplies, duplicate kitchen items, and labeled boxes. Keep medication, personal documents, medical information, and daily essentials at home.


**How Can I Create Room When an Older Parent Moves In?**
Clear a bedroom, downstairs room, or shared living area by putting away extra furniture and lower-use household items. Start with the spaces needed for daily routines, including the bedroom, bathroom, kitchen, and main living area.


**What Size Storage Unit Do I Need During a Family Care Transition?**
A 5×5 unit can fit boxes and small furniture, while a 10×10 unit can fit furniture and boxes from several rooms. Use the


[Public Storage size guide](https://www.publicstorage.com/size-guide) to compare sizes with your inventory.


**Is Drive-Up Storage Useful for Moving Furniture?**
[Drive-up storage](https://www.publicstorage.com/self-storage/drive-up-storage) can help with loading and unloading furniture, boxes, shelving, and other bulky household items from a vehicle.


**Can 24-Hour Storage Access Help With a Changing Care Schedule?**
[24/7](https://www.publicstorage.com/self-storage/24-hour-storage) access can help families retrieve household items around changing schedules. Confirm current access hours and unit availability at your selected location before reserving.
